Family Health

The Norwood scale: stages of male-pattern hair loss

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The Norwood scale describes common patterns of recession and crown thinning. It can support a conversation about male-pattern hair loss, but it does not predict an inevitable future or choose a treatment for you. The cause, pace of change and your preferences matter alongside the stage.

What the Norwood scale is for

The Norwood scale, also called the Hamilton–Norwood scale, describes common patterns of male-pattern hair loss. It gives clinicians and patients a shared way to talk about a receding front hairline and thinning on the crown, the upper area toward the back of the scalp. It is one classification system, not a test of general health or a measure of attractiveness.

The scale has seven main stages, along with variants. It can help document the starting pattern and compare photographs over time, but people do not necessarily move through every stage or progress at the same rate. A stage does not predict exactly how much hair you will lose or tell you which treatment you must choose.

Other systems describe different hair-loss patterns, including the more diffuse mid-scalp thinning often seen in female-pattern hair loss. A chart intended for male-pattern recession should not be forced onto every scalp. Diagnosis comes before using the number to discuss treatment.

Stages 1 to 3: the hairline and early crown changes

Stage 1 describes little or no visible recession. Stage 2 describes modest recession at the temples, often referred to as a mature hairline. That label is descriptive: it does not prove that the hairline will remain stable. Comparing a consistent photograph over time is more useful than repeatedly measuring a single corner in a mirror.

Stage 3 involves more pronounced recession at both temples, leaving an M-, V- or U-like outline. The receded areas may have very sparse hair or appear bare. This is more than a small change in the shape of the hairline, but assessment should still consider the full pattern and history.

The stage 3 vertex variant emphasizes thinning at the crown, sometimes with less marked front recession. “Vertex” means the top or crown, not the low back of the head where donor hair for a transplant is often found. Crown thinning and temple recession can develop at different rates.

Stages 4 to 7: larger areas become connected

At stage 4, recession at the front and hair loss at the crown are more substantial, with a band of hair still separating them. In stage 5, the two affected areas are larger and the intervening band is narrower and sparser. Lighting and hair length can make that band look different, so staging should not rely on one poorly lit photograph.

At stage 6, the front and crown areas of loss join as the separating bridge is lost. Stage 7 describes extensive loss on top, leaving a rim of hair around the sides and back. The density of the remaining rim varies; the stage does not guarantee that enough suitable donor hair is available for a particular transplant plan.

A higher stage describes greater visible loss in this pattern. It does not mean that a person needs surgery, that medicines cannot have any role or that choosing no treatment is unreasonable. Treatment goals and the condition of remaining hair are separate from the stage number.

The class A pattern is a variant

In the class A variant, the front hairline moves backward more continuously, without the usual separate crown patch and intervening island or bridge of hair. The point is the shape of the progression, not that it is a special diagnosis unrelated to androgenetic hair loss.

You may also see different labels or versions of a chart used by clinics. Ask which system they are using and what change they are trying to document. An online self-assigned stage should be treated as a starting description, especially when the pattern does not fit neatly into the drawings.

Confirm the cause before treating it

A clinician usually begins with the pattern, timing, family history, medicines, recent illnesses and an examination of the scalp. They may inspect hairs with magnification or perform a gentle pull test to understand shedding. Laboratory tests or a scalp biopsy are considered when the history or examination points to another cause, rather than being necessary for everyone.

Sudden heavy shedding, sharply defined patches, broken hairs, scalp pain, marked itching, inflammation or scarring deserves assessment rather than being labeled a Norwood stage. Infection, alopecia areata, traction, medication effects and shedding after illness are among other possibilities. More than one type of hair loss can occur at once.

Unexpected loss at a very young age or a pattern accompanied by other hormonal symptoms also needs an individualized review. A familiar family pattern can be useful information, but it does not rule out a second condition. Bring photographs and a timeline if you have them; do not delay assessment simply to collect a perfect series.

Genes, hormones and the hair growth cycle

Male-pattern hair loss reflects inherited susceptibility of certain follicles to androgens, especially dihydrotestosterone, or DHT. Genes from either side of the family can contribute. It is not determined only by the maternal grandfather, and relatives may start losing hair at different ages or develop different patterns.

Hair normally cycles through growth, transition and rest before shedding and replacement. In susceptible scalp areas, follicles gradually produce finer, shorter hairs through a process called miniaturization, and the growth phase becomes shorter. This is different from all hairs suddenly stopping production at the same moment.

The pattern does not necessarily mean that blood testosterone is abnormally high. Nor is there a universal two-year deadline after which every quiet follicle becomes permanently impossible to treat. Earlier discussion can help preserve existing hair, but promises based on an exact inactivity cutoff oversimplify a variable biological process.

Topical minoxidil: expectations and routine

Topical minoxidil is available without a prescription in many places and can help reduce ongoing loss or improve growth in some people. It is applied to the scalp according to the particular product’s directions. Different formulations and local labels may have different instructions; using more than directed does not guarantee better results.

Expect a gradual trial rather than a change within days. A visible response may take several months, and some people do not respond. Full restoration of the original density is unlikely. The benefit generally depends on continued use, so discuss the time, cost and practicality before starting.

Scalp irritation, itching or unwanted hair growth can occur. Ask for advice about troublesome reactions and follow the product’s warnings. Oral minoxidil is a different, prescription treatment with systemic risks and should not be substituted for a topical product without medical supervision. A dermatologist may combine treatments when appropriate.

Finasteride: benefits and important adverse effects

Finasteride is a prescription medicine that reduces formation of DHT and can slow male-pattern loss; some people also gain density. Response varies with the person, outcome measured and length of treatment. A claim that exactly 88% stop losing hair or 66% regrow it should not be treated as an individual guarantee.

Several months may be needed to judge benefit, and continued use is usually required to maintain it. Before prescribing, the clinician should review medical history, other medicines and the possible effects on sexual function and mood. Do not obtain an uncertain product online simply because a photograph appears to show dramatic regrowth.

UK MHRA warnings include sexual dysfunction, depression and suicidal thoughts; sexual effects have been reported to persist after stopping. If taking finasteride for hair loss and depression or suicidal thoughts develop, stop it and seek medical advice. Immediate danger or an inability to stay safe requires emergency support. Report sexual side effects to the prescriber so the treatment can be reviewed.

Laser devices and other advertised treatments

Low-level light or laser devices are sold as caps, combs and other home products. Some studies suggest benefit with particular devices, but the quality of evidence, dose schedules and results differ. A marketing clearance or an impressive before-and-after photograph does not establish that every device is effective or that it will work for your pattern.

Ask about evidence for the exact product, realistic changes in density, how long treatment must continue, eye/skin precautions and the total cost. A blanket statement that all lasers are proven or all are disproven is less useful than a device-specific discussion. They should not delay diagnosis of painful, inflamed or rapidly changing hair loss.

Clinics may also offer injections or combinations of procedures. Ask which parts are established for your diagnosis and which remain uncertain, and how improvement will be measured. Supplements are not a general solution to inherited patterned loss unless there is a relevant deficiency or another specific indication.

Transplantation, older operations and camouflage

A hair transplant moves suitable donor follicles, usually from the sides or back, into selected areas of loss. It redistributes available hair rather than creating an unlimited new supply. Suitability depends on donor density, the pattern’s stability, scalp health, expectations and the likelihood of further loss. Scarring, complications, cost and possible later procedures belong in the discussion.

Older descriptions of treatment may include scalp reduction, in which bald skin is removed and hair-bearing areas are brought closer, or tissue expansion, in which an implanted device stretches skin over time. These are not routine next steps for everyone with advanced male-pattern loss. Their role is specialized, and a source’s fixed three-to-four-week timetable should not be used as a universal surgical plan.

Scalp micropigmentation creates small tattooed marks to suggest a closely shaved appearance; it does not grow hair. Wigs, hairpieces, styling changes and cosmetic fibers are other options, depending on the pattern and your preferences. Ask about pigment change, infection, touch-ups or maintenance where relevant. Choosing camouflage or no treatment is a valid decision at any stage.

Make the scale useful without letting it define you

If you want treatment, agree on a realistic goal: slowing further loss, improving density, changing the hairline’s appearance or feeling more comfortable with your look. Use photographs taken with similar lighting, angle and hair length at sensible intervals to judge progress with the clinician. Daily comparisons can exaggerate normal differences.

Review benefits and adverse effects at the agreed time rather than switching products every few weeks. The speed of progression varies, and neither minoxidil nor finasteride guarantees permanent prevention after treatment stops. A long-term plan should account for maintenance as well as the initial result.

Hair loss can affect confidence, and those feelings deserve attention. You do not need to minimize distress, but you also do not need to treat a stage number as a measure of age, health or worth. Ask for emotional support if worry is interfering with everyday life, and make treatment choices around your priorities.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Staging describes appearance; assessment establishes the cause and suitability of treatment.

Medicines and procedures have variable benefits and risks, and ongoing maintenance often matters.

How BeMama can help

Bring a timeline and consistent photographs to a qualified clinician. Discuss what change would feel worthwhile to you, along with cost, maintenance and adverse effects.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for sudden, patchy, painful or inflamed loss. Depression or suicidal thoughts during finasteride hair-loss treatment require stopping it and seeking medical advice; immediate danger needs emergency support.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The scale includes seven main stages and variants; progression is not inevitable.
  • The crown is different from the low back of the scalp.
  • DHT susceptibility can be inherited from either parent.
  • No universal two-year inactivity deadline or fixed success percentage predicts your response.
  • Surgery, camouflage and no treatment are choices, not requirements of a stage.

Frequently asked questions

Does stage 2 mean I will eventually reach stage 7?

No. Progression and speed vary. The stage describes the current pattern, not a fixed future.

What does vertex mean?

It means the top or crown of the scalp, rather than the low back of the head.

How is the class A pattern different?

The front hairline moves backward more continuously, without the usual separate crown patch and intervening bridge of hair.

Can the chart diagnose sudden patchy loss?

No. Sudden, patchy, painful or inflamed loss needs assessment for other causes rather than a stage assignment.

Is male-pattern loss inherited only from my mother?

No. Genetic susceptibility can come from either side of the family, and relatives can have different patterns.

Do all follicles become untreatable after two years?

No. There is no universal two-year cutoff. Earlier treatment may help preserve hair, but response is individual.

Will minoxidil restore all my hair?

Usually not. It can help some people over several months, and benefit generally depends on continued use.

What if finasteride affects my mood?

If depression or suicidal thoughts develop during hair-loss treatment, stop it and seek medical advice. If you cannot stay safe, use emergency support immediately.

Are all laser devices equally effective?

No. Evidence and treatment schedules differ. Ask about the exact device and realistic outcomes before spending money.

Does a high stage mean I must have a transplant?

No. Suitability and preferences matter. Medicines, camouflage or no treatment may also be reasonable choices.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
